about:
A PROJECT-DEFINED EDITORIAL EQUIVALENT, NOT AN EXTERNAL SYLLABUS. NOTHING IN THIS FILE MAY BE ATTRIBUTED TO ANY GUJARATI EXAMINING OR LANGUAGE BODY. core/exam-levels.json records gujarati as exam 'no widely-sat ladder', basis 'editorial', and it carries NO caveat. Gujarat's state school syllabi and the Gujarati Sahitya Parishad examinations exist, but they are built for children schooled in Gujarati or for literary attainment rather than for an adult second-language learner against CEFR can-do descriptors, and neither was consulted. Read 'A1' here as the CEFR descriptor and as a measuring stick this project built for itself.

EXAM ENVELOPE: A PRE-A1 TASK SHAPE EXISTS AND AN A1 ONE DOES NOT. gujarati/task-shapes/ holds exactly one file, pre-a1.json. gujarati/assessment.json declares all seven rungs and points at task-shapes/a1.json and at fourteen mocks; task-shapes/a1.json does not exist, gujarati/mocks/ does not exist, and every artifact assessment.json names except pre-a1.json is missing. So this file cannot cite a paper part the way the Punjabi inventory can, and it says so rather than implying an envelope it does not have.

SEARCH FOR AN EXTERNAL SOURCE: NOT SEARCHED, BY INSTRUCTION. The project settled at HL-C287/HL-C290 that the proxy derivation is the method for tracks with no sat ladder, and the search was deliberately not redone for Gujarati. Saying so is what keeps 'we did not look' from reading as 'there is nothing to find'.

THE REGISTER COLUMN IS DERIVED FROM LESSON BODIES, NOT FROM FRONTMATTER, AND THAT IS ITSELF THE FINDING. All 228 lessons carry register: neutral, so the frontmatter asserts this track makes no register distinction whatever. It does: the tu / tame contrast is taught explicitly, compared to French vous, given a hard rule for first meetings, and then propagated into the copula, the possessive and the farewell -- four coupled places, none of them visible in a frontmatter field. An inventory that had trusted the frontmatter would have reported no register column at all.

GENDER IS THIS TRACK'S OWN COLUMN. Gujarati keeps the Sanskrit neuter that Hindi and Punjabi lost, so it has THREE genders, and five of the corpus's eight grammar atoms are about gender -- the neuter -u tell, the -vu infinitive being neuter, the fact that the ending does NOT settle it, gender shifting during inheritance, and an infinitive agreeing with its OBJECT. That is the deepest grammar in the track by a wide margin and it gets a column of its own.
source: PROJECT-DEFINED. LEVEL PROXY: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json, the DELE/PCIC-sourced Spanish A1 point set, used for the STRUCTURE of what an A1 learner must handle. Its own source is the Instituto Cervantes Plan Curricular inventories. The proxy supplies the LEVEL and the shape of the columns; every Gujarati exponent is this project's choice, and every point records which Spanish point or points it was derived from.

anchors.title: code/learning/human-languages/core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json
anchors.note: The DELE/PCIC-sourced Spanish A1 point set, used for the STRUCTURE of what an A1 learner must handle. Spanish is a proxy for LEVEL, never for grammar: each point was read as 'what must an A1 learner be able to do here', and the Gujarati exponent that carries the same load was then chosen. Where Gujarati carries the load with machinery Spanish does not have -- a three-way gender, a neuter infinitive, a dative-liking construction, postpositions -- the point is restated around the Gujarati machinery and its Spanish origin recorded in derivedFrom.

anchors.title: Council of Europe, CEFR Companion Volume
anchors.note: Supplies the meaning of 'A1' as a can-do band. It describes what a learner can DO and names no language's forms, which is why a second, language-shaped source was needed.

anchors.title: gujarati/lessons/ as merged on main
anchors.note: 228 lessons, all schema_version 2, introducing 219 atoms. Every probe in this file names an atom drawn from that set and was checked mechanically against it before the file was written; no probe names an id a future lesson is expected to introduce. Note the shape of that atom set: 68 are script atoms and 27 are etymologies, so the count is larger than the usable A1 language in it.

anchors.title: this project's judgement about Gujarati
anchors.note: Where a Spanish point has no single Gujarati exponent, the choice of which Gujarati form carries the load is this project's and is defended in the point's own note. The clearest cases are giving gender a column of its own, deriving the register column from lesson bodies rather than the uniformly-neutral frontmatter, and declining to claim a Sanskritic/native register axis on the strength of one concept atom.

communicative-functions.source: Derived from the PCIC functional inventory by way of core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json.
communicative-functions.note: Every Spanish functional subsection was walked. Partial because the answers are this project's editorial choices rather than an examining body's list, and because there is no A1 task shape and no mock to check an exponent against.

grammar.source: Derived from the PCIC grammar inventory by way of core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json.
grammar.note: Every Spanish A1 grammar category was answered, including the ones whose Gujarati answer is that the category is absent from the corpus. Partial because a Gujarati-shaped grammar inventory would enumerate categories Spanish never raises -- the neuter, the ergative, the oblique -- and this file reaches those only where a Spanish point pointed at them, and because the corpus has eight grammar atoms in total.

phonology-orthography.source: Derived from the PCIC orthography inventory, plus this track's own script and sound-change lessons.
phonology-orthography.note: Script closure over the CORPUS is exact and holds even over lesson bodies -- 43 of 43 characters taught, zero leaks. Closure over the ALPHABET is about two thirds: fourteen letters and all ten digits are never taught. Partial for that, for the untaught punctuation, and because the sound points are historical sound CHANGE rather than pronunciation.

lexicon.source: Derived from the PCIC notional inventories by way of core/exam-inventory-es-a1.json.
lexicon.note: All twenty Spanish specific-notion areas were walked. Roughly 48 concrete content nouns exist in the track, and clothes, colours, animals and health are at absolute zero. The uncovered areas are enumerated rather than omitted.

probeSemantics: A probe is the set of atoms whose presence in the corpus demonstrates the point. ALL of them must be introduced for the point to count: a point covered by half its atoms is not covered, because a candidate asked for the whole of something does not get partial credit for half of it. probe: null means nothing in the corpus corresponds to the point, and every null carries a note naming what is missing -- those notes are a work queue and are written as one.

points.label: proper nouns: a personal name, given in an introduction
place names: the town you live in, and the country you are from
points.note: shahar ('city'), gaam ('village') and ghar ('home') are taught as CATEGORIES of place; not one settlement name exists. Ahmedabad appears once as an unlabelled example sentence inside GU-C05-rahevun with no atom, and there is no word for a country and no Gujarat or Bharat anywhere. Three Spanish points rest on this.

points.label: common nouns naming stretches of time
points.note: divas ('day') and mahino -- which is the WORD for month and not any month's name.

points.label: number: forming a plural noun
points.note: NOT TAUGHT ANYWHERE. The word 'plural' occurs in two lessons and in both it means tame being grammatically plural as a courtesy. There is no plural noun form, no rule, and no plural atom.

points.label: natural gender by separate words: bhai against bahen
points.note: and the etymology the track hangs on the pair: bhai is the plainest cousin of English brother, and bahen is not the cousin of sister.

points.category: Ling (grammatical gender, of which Gujarati has three)
points.label: Gujarati nouns come in three genders, not two
points.note: maaru / maaro / maari, taught on the possessive in chapter 2. Gujarati keeps the Sanskrit neuter that Hindi and Punjabi lost, so a learner arriving from either has a third box to learn.

points.category: Ling (grammatical gender, of which Gujarati has three)
points.label: the nasalised -u ending is the neuter's tell
points.note: Taught on modhu ('mouth'). The one reliable surface clue the language gives.

points.category: Ling (grammatical gender, of which Gujarati has three)
points.label: the -vu infinitive is itself neuter
points.note: Which is why every verb in this track is cited as hovu, javu, khaavu -- the dictionary form is a neuter noun.

points.category: Ling (grammatical gender, of which Gujarati has three)
points.label: but the ending does NOT settle it: -i is not always feminine
points.note: Taught on rotli. The track is unusually honest here: it teaches the clue and then teaches that the clue fails.

points.category: Ling (grammatical gender, of which Gujarati has three)
points.label: a word can change gender on its way into the language
points.note: Taught on kaan ('ear'), a word Sanskrit itself could not settle.

points.category: Ling (grammatical gender, of which Gujarati has three)
points.label: the infinitive agrees with its OBJECT
points.note: madad karvi, not karvu, because madad is feminine. A genuinely difficult agreement rule, taught at A1, and the fifth of the track's eight grammar atoms to be about gender.

points.category: Ling (grammatical gender, of which Gujarati has three)
points.label: the present tense carries no gender at all
points.note: Stated explicitly in GU-C07-javun. Worth its own point because the learner has just been taught five gender rules and needs to know where they stop.

points.label: qualifying adjectives, and evaluating something as good
points.note: saaru ('good, okay, fine') is the ONLY adjective in the track. Four Spanish evaluation points rest on it -- general evaluation, quality, correctness -- and there is no word for bad or wrong, so evaluation runs one way only.

points.label: the adjective agrees in gender
points.note: The gender machinery is taught in depth for nouns, possessives and infinitives, and never for an adjective -- saaru/saari/saaro is never contrasted, because there is no second adjective to contrast it with.

points.label: position: the adjective stands before its noun
points.note: Never stated. The corpus contains no adjective-plus-noun phrase.

points.label: relational adjectives: where a person is from
points.note: No gentilic.

points.label: degree: very, quite, a bit
points.note: bahu is not taught, nor any other degree word. Four Spanish points on one gap.

points.label: colour as a quality
points.note: ZERO colour terms in 228 lessons -- no laal, no nilu, nothing.

points.label: attractiveness, ease, difficulty, age of a thing
points.note: None taught. With one adjective in the whole track this is where most of the Spanish qualitative points land.

points.category: Nirdeshak (definiteness, and the article Gujarati does not have)
points.label: Gujarati has no article: a bare noun is definite or indefinite by context
points.note: Correct for Gujarati, and never stated. ek ('one') is taught as a numeral and never as 'a'.

points.category: Nirdeshak (definiteness, and the article Gujarati does not have)
points.label: no article contractions exist, because there is no article to contract
points.note: Enumerated rather than dropped so the walk is total.

points.label: aa and te: this and that
points.note: NOT TAUGHT. aa is taught only as the LETTER aa (GU-SCRIPT-AA-01), never as the word 'this'; te appears as a free word in exactly one lesson, inside a copula recitation. Three Spanish points on one gap, and it leaves the track's 48 nouns with nothing to point at them.

points.label: ahin and tyaan: here and there
points.note: Not taught.

points.label: second person: tu and tame, taught as one contrast
points.note: The pair is taught as a register choice with the rule 'for a first meeting, use tame', and the copula is drilled to match it.

points.label: third person: te -- he, she, it
points.note: NOT TAUGHT. te occurs as a free word in one file, inside the copula paradigm recitation in GU-C02-chhe, with no atom of its own. Nothing can be said about anyone absent.

points.label: plural pronouns: ame, aapne, teo
points.note: NOT TAUGHT -- zero occurrences. 'We' survives only inside the lexicalised future malishun, 'we will meet'.

points.label: the oblique pronoun: mane, 'to me'
points.note: Taught only inside the gamvu construction, never as a general form.

points.label: interrogative pronouns: shun
points.note: shun ('what') is taught. kon ('who') is named once in a prose aside and never introduced.

points.label: the relative je
points.note: Zero occurrences as a word -- the single apparent hit is aavje, the familiar imperative of the goodbye. Three Spanish points open.

points.label: reflexive and exclamative
points.note: Neither taught.

points.label: maaru: my, in all three genders
the genitive no / ni / nu, between two nouns
points.note: NOT TAUGHT. nu returns zero occurrences as a word; no and ni appear only as substrings of mahino, keri and baari. So 'my friend's book' cannot be built although both nouns are taught, and taaru/tamaru have no atom either.

points.label: having something
points.note: Gujarati says 'to me X is'. Neither the frame nor a general dative is taught.

points.label: why be begins with b and tran kept its r
points.note: Five atoms on two numbers. The track uses them to teach learned restoration -- a sound that was lost and then put back by scholars -- which is real historical linguistics at A1.

points.label: cardinals six to ten
points.note: THE COUNT STOPS AT FIVE. chha, saat, aath, nav and das return zero hits. Ages, prices, times and quantities are all closed above five.

points.label: counting past ten
points.note: Follows from GU-A1-NUM-03.

points.label: ordinals
points.note: Not taught.

points.label: relative quantity and sufficiency
points.note: Neither vadhu nor ochhu nor bas is taught. Five Spanish points on one gap; there is no way to answer 'how much'.

points.label: measures: size, distance and weight
points.note: Nothing.

points.label: the Gujarati digits
points.note: NOT ONE DIGIT IS TAUGHT OR USED. A character census over every headword and every lesson body finds no codepoint in the Gujarati digit range at all, so a learner cannot read a price, a house number or a date.

points.label: postpositions come AFTER the noun
points.note: GU-C05-rahevun has a grammar lens headed 'in comes after the noun' and that SECTION INTRODUCES NOTHING -- its introduces list is empty, and the lesson's only atom is the verb. So the principle is explained in prose and is not an atom, and -ma otherwise appears only inside majaama.

points.label: -ne: the dative and the marked object
points.note: Taught only for the gamvu construction, as mane/tamne, never as a general marker.

points.label: -thi: from, by
points.note: Zero occurrences.

points.label: -ma: in, at
points.note: See GU-A1-CASE-01: explained, never an atom.

points.label: par and the spatial postpositions
points.note: Zero. No word for on, under, behind or in front of.

points.label: with, and the instrumental
points.note: Not taught.

points.label: the ergative -e
points.note: Not taught, and moot while there is no past tense -- but Gujarati's past cannot be taught without it.

points.label: the -vu infinitive, which is how every verb is named
the present: stem plus a person ending plus the copula
points.note: hun jaaun chhun / tame jao chho / te jaay chhe -- taught as a three-form paradigm, which is more than most tracks in this series manage.

points.label: the copula chhe, and its person forms
points.note: chhun / chhe / chho, plus the etymology from a root meaning 'to dwell'. Five Spanish ser/estar points land here because Gujarati has one copula and no choice to make.

points.label: the past tense
points.note: ENTIRELY ABSENT, AND IT TAKES EIGHT SPANISH POINTS WITH IT. Two lessons forward-reference it -- saying gender lives in the past tense -- and the memorised aanand thayo contains an unanalysed past participle. Nothing teaches it.

points.label: the future: the -ishun ending
points.note: Taught for the first plural only, inside a farewell. 'We will meet' is sayable; 'I will go' is not.

points.label: the progressive
points.note: Not taught.

points.label: the imperative
points.note: NOT TAUGHT as a form. aavjo is named in prose as 'the polite imperative of aavvu' and its atom is a lexical goodbye; the word 'imperative' occurs in one file. There is no other imperative in the corpus -- no come, sit, give me, or repeat please.

points.label: a noun plus karvu, the way Gujarati makes new verbs
points.note: kaam karvu and madad karvi -- and the second is where the object-gender rule is taught.

points.label: verbs of motion: javu and aavvu
verbs of perception and knowing: jovu, jaanvu
points.note: and the minimal pair with javu, which is one vowel sign away.

points.label: verbs of the mind: vicharvu, samajvu
verbs of the page: vanchvu, lakhvu
points.note: and the etymology that vanchvu once meant 'to make a voice', which is what reading was before it was silent.

points.label: verbs of exchange: levu, puchhvu, madad karvi
verbs of everyday living: khaavu, rahevu, bolvu
liking: mane X game chhe
points.note: Gujarati's answer to gustar, and the corpus notes the verb is built on a root meaning 'to go' -- what pleases you GOES to you.

points.label: ability and wanting
points.note: Neither shakvu nor joie is taught. Five Spanish points about what a learner can and wants to do have no Gujarati form here.

points.label: na: the bare no
points.note: Taught as the second half of the haa/naa pair, and that is the entire negative resource of the track.

points.label: nathi: negating a sentence
points.note: ZERO OCCURRENCES IN 228 FILES, in script or romanisation. This is the starkest single finding in the file: a learner cannot say 'I don't understand', 'it isn't', or 'no, I don't'. Gujarati's ordinary sentence negator is simply not in the corpus.

points.label: nahin, and the fixed phrase that carries it
points.note: vaandho nahin -- 'no objection'. nahin occurs in five lessons and every one of them is inside this chunk, so the word is in the learner's mouth and not in their grammar.

points.label: negative coordination and refusal
points.note: Depends on the missing coordinator and the missing negator together.

points.label: kem: how, and also why
points.note: One word doing two jobs, which is a genuine economy and is taught as one.

points.label: kon: who
points.note: Named once, in a single prose aside in GU-C02-shun about the k- question family. Never an atom.

points.label: kyaan: where
points.note: Same single prose aside, same line of the same file. This is the one that closes 'where are you from' -- a core A1 identity function -- in a track that teaches city, village and home.

points.label: kyaare: when
points.note: Same prose aside.

points.label: kevi rite: how, in what manner
points.note: Zero occurrences.

points.label: ketlaa: how much, how many
points.note: Zero occurrences.

points.label: the yes-or-no question
points.note: Covered by example -- the how-are-you question is the model -- and by no rule.

points.label: asking for confirmation: a tag question
points.note: Not taught.

points.label: polarity: yes and no as one-word answers
manner: well, badly
points.note: Not taught.

points.label: place deictics: here, there
points.note: See GU-A1-DEM-02.

points.label: connective adverbs: also, neither
points.note: pan as 'also' is not taught.

points.label: certainty, doubt and possibility
points.note: Nothing. Five Spanish points about certainty and hedging have no Gujarati exponent in the corpus.

points.label: the dative-liking sentence: mane X game chhe
points.note: The longest structure the track teaches.

points.label: the declarative, affirmative and negative
points.note: Affirmative only -- see GU-A1-NEG-02 for why the negative half does not exist.

points.label: the question, with and without an asking word
the existential sentence: there is, there are
points.note: Not taught.

points.label: the vocative: addressing somebody
points.note: No term of address and no vocative particle. A learner cannot open a conversation by naming anyone.

points.label: the noun phrase: more than one word before the verb
points.note: With one adjective, no genitive and no demonstrative, the track's noun phrases are single nouns.

points.label: and: joining two nouns, and joining two clauses
points.note: ABSENT. ane returns ZERO occurrences in 228 files, in script and in romanisation. The word does not exist in this corpus. A learner cannot say 'tea and milk' although both are taught in the same chapter.

points.label: or: offering two alternatives
points.note: athava is absent, and ke never occurs as a standalone word -- all 25 apparent hits are inside kem or keri.

points.label: but: setting one thing against another
points.note: pan and parantu are both absent.

points.label: distributive: one thing, then the other
points.note: Absent.

points.label: because: giving a reason
points.note: kemke is absent. kem is taught and can mean 'why', so the question is askable and the answer is not.

points.label: that-clauses: saying what somebody said or thinks
points.note: The complementiser ke never occurs as a word. vicharvu, samajvu and jaanvu are all taught and none of them can be given anything to think, understand or know.

points.label: when: locating one event against another
points.note: jyaare is absent.

points.label: if: the conditional clause
points.note: jo is absent -- all 16 apparent hits are inside aavjo or the stem of jovu.

points.label: in order to, and therefore
points.note: maate and tethi are both absent.

points.label: the relative clause with je
points.note: Absent. Enumerated here as well as at GU-A1-PRON-07 because the Spanish inventory files relatives under both.

points.label: any two-clause sentence at all
points.note: THE COLUMN IS EMPTY, 0 OF 11. Ten joining devices were searched in Gujarati script and in romanisation across every headword, gloss and body; every raw match was checked in context and every one is a substring artefact. The track's own roadmap agrees -- its backlog item 2.2 asks for negation and basic question patterns -- so this is measured debt the authors already suspect, now enumerated.

points.label: the parts of the day: morning, midday, evening, night
points.note: Four words, each heard before it is read, and then bundled into a four-skill performance. The track's strongest lexical set.

points.label: tomorrow and yesterday
points.note: kaal means BOTH, and the corpus says so. Gujarati disambiguates it by TENSE -- which this track does not teach (GU-A1-V-04) -- so an exam item testing 'yesterday' is unanswerable from this corpus. Recorded as covered because the word is taught, with the caveat stated.

points.label: the day and the month as spans
the days of the week
points.note: Not one weekday name.

points.label: the months by name
points.note: mahino is the common noun only; no month is named.

points.label: the seasons
points.note: Zero occurrences of ritu or any season.

points.label: telling the clock time
points.note: vaagye is absent, and impossible above five in any case.

points.label: asking and giving an age
points.note: Zero hits for 'how old' or 'years old', and no number above five to answer with.

points.label: before and after, and locating an event in time
points.note: Nothing, and it would need a postposition on a time word -- which GU-A1-CASE-04 records as unavailable.

points.label: greet
points.note: namaste, which the track teaches as both hello and goodbye.

points.label: greet by the time of day
points.note: savaar and raat are taught as bare time NOUNS; no good-morning or good-night greeting is built from them.

points.label: respond to a greeting, and say how you are
points.note: majaa, and the reply hun majaamaa chhun.

points.label: respond to an introduction
points.note: tamne maline aanand thayo. The phrase contains a past participle the track never analyses, which is why GU-A1-V-04 matters.

points.label: apologise
points.note: NOT TAUGHT AT ALL. Zero hits for maaf, kshama, sorry or excuse me across 228 lessons. There is no way to apologise or to get someone's attention, which closes both a courtesy function and a repair strategy.

points.label: say please, and ask for something
points.note: The one request pattern in the corpus is NOUN plus meherbani karine, taught as a rider on paani. There is no verb-based request and no 'can I'.

points.label: ask for help
points.note: The verb is taught; the frame that would ask for help is not -- see GU-A1-V-16.

points.label: respond to a request: all right
take leave
points.note: aavjo -- literally '[please] come [again]' -- plus pachha malishun and kaale malishun. Three farewells, and the track explains that Gujarati says come rather than go.

points.label: disagree, and say you do not know or understand
points.note: OPEN, AND IT IS THE MISSING NEGATOR. samajvu and jaanvu are both taught and neither can be negated, because nathi does not appear in the corpus. 'I don't understand' is arguably the most necessary A1 utterance and it cannot be said.

points.label: give an opinion or an evaluation
points.note: OPEN, AND IT IS THE COMPLEMENTISER. 'I think that ...' needs the ke that GU-A1-JOIN-06 records as absent, and the evaluation vocabulary beyond saaru does not exist. Five Spanish points on one gap.

points.label: show one is following: I see, right
give an order or instruction
points.note: See GU-A1-V-07.

points.label: offer, invite, accept and decline
points.note: haa and naa can answer, and no offer or invitation frame exists to answer.

points.label: grant or refuse permission
points.note: Nothing.

points.label: state a plan or intention
points.note: The future ending exists for one person only.

points.label: express a wish or a preference
points.note: See GU-A1-V-16.

points.label: congratulate, toast, offer condolences
points.note: Nothing taught.

points.label: address somebody by name or title
points.note: See GU-A1-S-07.

points.label: ask for a person, and ask somebody to be quiet
points.note: Neither is taught; both need the third-person pronoun and the imperative.

points.label: say how you feel physically
points.note: majaa answers 'how are you' as a formula. No word for tired, ill, hungry or happy.

points.label: welcome somebody
points.note: swagat is absent. The house vocabulary is taught and no welcome is.

points.label: the face: eye, ear, nose, mouth
the hand
points.note: Five body words in all: the face and one hand. No head, leg, stomach or back.

points.label: physical characteristics and personality
points.note: Nothing -- and with one adjective in the track there is nothing to describe anyone with.

points.label: family: brother, sister, the family itself
points.note: Three kin words, and the track notes kutumb is a Dravidian borrowing into Indo-Aryan. NO MOTHER, FATHER, SON, DAUGHTER, WIFE OR HUSBAND is taught.

points.label: celebrations and occasions
points.note: Nothing.

points.label: drink: water, tea, milk
points.note: and the cha/tea isogloss -- which word a language uses depends on whether it met tea overland or by sea.

points.label: the plate: rice, lentils, vegetable, oil, mango, flatbread
points.note: Six foods bundled into an oral performance. The track's best domain.

points.label: meals of the day, and eating out
points.note: No meal name and no word for a restaurant.

points.label: the house: home, door, window, chair, key, lamp
housing as a transaction, and domestic activity
points.note: Nothing.

points.label: places in a town: market, temple, shop, school, road, city, village
points.note: Seven places, two performance bundles. Unusually strong, and it makes the missing 'where' at GU-A1-Q-04 more costly rather than less.

points.label: money
points.note: paisa is taught. No price, no rupee, no buying or selling verb -- so GU-A1-LEX-15 is the gap this leaves.

points.label: paying, prices, buying and selling
points.note: Nothing, and with no number above five the shopping scenario is closed twice over.

points.label: clothing and footwear
points.note: ZERO. No garment word of any kind.

points.label: animals
points.note: ZERO. No animal word in any atom.

points.label: rain, and the river
points.note: varsaad ('rain') is the only weather word. There is no hot or cold, and no way to say it is raining.

points.label: plants and the countryside
points.note: Nothing.

points.label: geography: country, town, capital
points.note: See GU-A1-N-02.

points.label: study: book, paper, school, reading, writing
the education system: teachers, timetable, examinations
points.note: Nothing. No profession noun of any kind exists in the track -- no teacher, no student, no doctor.

points.label: professions, workplaces and conditions of work
points.note: Nothing.

points.label: travel, transport and accommodation

Gujarati dropped the top line Devanagari keeps
points.note: Taught on the numbers, and it is the single fastest way to tell Gujarati from Hindi on a page.

points.label: the independent vowel letters
points.note: Five of them.

points.label: the dependent vowel signs
points.note: Nine signs, including the vocalic r that only Sanskrit borrowings need.

points.label: the anusvara, and what it does inside a word
the retroflexes and the distinctively Indic letters
reading a whole known word back off the page
points.note: The track's whole-word spelling atoms, which follow the word being HEARD in an earlier lesson.

points.label: the fourteen letters of the alphabet the track never teaches
points.note: MEASURED TWO WAYS, AND THE TWO ANSWERS DIFFER. Against the CORPUS closure is EXACT and unusually so: 43 distinct Gujarati characters appear in headwords, all 43 are taught, and extending the census to every lesson BODY still finds 43 and zero untaught -- the track never leaks a glyph even in a prose example. Against the ALPHABET it is about two thirds: fourteen letters are never taught and never used, including the everyday DDA, PHA, O and short I, plus the visarga, the candrabindu and the nukta. A reading paper drawn from real signage would be unreadable.

points.label: the Gujarati digits
points.note: NOT ONE. The character census finds no codepoint in the digit range anywhere in the corpus. See GU-A1-NUM-08.

points.label: capital letters, and written accentuation
points.note: Gujarati has neither. Enumerated rather than dropped so a reader comparing the files sees the answer.

points.label: punctuation
points.note: Gujarati uses the European marks alongside the danda, and no lesson teaches any of them.

points.label: abbreviations and initialisms
points.note: Nothing taught.

points.label: Sanskrit y- became Gujarati j-
points.note: Taught on javu. The track uses sound change as a vocabulary aid: knowing the law makes the next word cheaper.

points.label: the Prakrit p-to-v softening
points.note: Taught on aavvu.

points.label: how dhy became jjh became j
points.note: Taught on samajvu.

points.label: how dv became bb became b
points.note: Taught on be, the number two.

points.label: long and short vowels as a meaning difference
points.note: The matras are taught as shapes; no lesson says length changes the word.

points.label: word stress
points.note: Not taught.

points.label: tu against tame: courtesy expressed as plurality
points.note: MEASURED FROM THE LESSON BODIES, NOT THE FRONTMATTER -- and that distinction is the finding. All 228 lessons carry register: neutral, so the frontmatter says this track makes no register distinction at all. It does: GU-C02-tu-tame teaches the contrast explicitly, compares it to French vous, and gives the rule 'for a first meeting, use tame'.

points.label: the copula has to match the pronoun you chose
points.note: tame kem chho against tu kem chhe, drilled as a paired rule. The register choice is not decorative -- it changes the verb.

points.label: the possessive matches it too
points.note: tamaru against taaru, explained inside the name question.

points.label: the farewell has a familiar form as well
points.note: aavjo against aavje -- a lexicalised imperative pair, and the fourth place the same axis surfaces.

points.label: a Sanskritic or a native word: which register a borrowing lands in
points.note: The track teaches learned borrowing as a concept, on kutumb. It does NOT build a Sanskritic-against-everyday doublet column the way the Punjabi track does, and this file does not claim one -- one atom is a concept, not an axis.
